---
title: "Readings — Amplification"
---

Reading is optional but each item is here for a reason. Start with the two marked **start
here** if you read nothing else.

## Papers

**Saiki RK, Gelfand DH, Stoffel S, et al. (1988).** *Primer-directed enzymatic amplification of
DNA with a thermostable DNA polymerase.* Science 239:487–491.
[doi:10.1126/science.2448875](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.2448875)

> The paper that made PCR practical by replacing the heat-labile enzyme. Read it for the
> reasoning behind the thermal cycle, which every other method in this deck is a reply to.

**Aird D, Ross MG, Chen WS, et al. (2011).** *Analyzing and minimizing PCR amplification bias
in Illumina sequencing libraries.* Genome Biology 12:R18.
[doi:10.1186/gb-2011-12-2-r18](https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2011-12-2-r18) — **start here**

> Measures what PCR does to coverage and shows how changing the protocol reduces it. Look at the
> GC-content plots.

**Kebschull JM, Zador AM (2015).** *Sources of PCR-induced distortions in high-throughput
sequencing data sets.* Nucleic Acids Research, article gkv717.
[doi:10.1093/nar/gkv717](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv717) — **start here**

> Separates the kinds of damage PCR does: errors, template switching and chimeras, and
> amplification bias. Look at which of them grow with cycle number.

**Dean FB, Hosono S, Fang L, et al. (2002).** *Comprehensive human genome amplification using
multiple displacement amplification.* PNAS 99:5261–5266.
[doi:10.1073/pnas.082089499](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.082089499)

> The human-DNA case for phi29 and random primers. Compare the coverage evenness it reports with
> what you would expect from PCR.

**Zong C, Lu S, Chapman AR, Xie XS (2012).** *Genome-wide detection of single-nucleotide and
copy-number variations of a single human cell.* Science 338:1622–1626.
[doi:10.1126/science.1229164](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1229164)

> MALBAC, designed to make the amplification quasi-linear. Compare the amplification diagram
> with the branching picture of MDA.

**Schmidt M, Schwarzwaelder K, Bartholomae C, et al. (2007).** *High-resolution insertion-site
analysis by linear amplification-mediated PCR (LAM-PCR).* Nature Methods 4:1051–1057.
[doi:10.1038/nmeth1103](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth1103)

> Linear amplification used to find where a vector went in human cells. Look at why the first
> step is a single-primer reaction.

**Potter CJ, Luo L (2010).** *Splinkerette PCR for mapping transposable elements in
Drosophila.* PLoS ONE 5:e10168.
[doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0010168](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0010168)

> The splinkerette design, and a comparison with the inverse PCR it replaces. The organism is
> the fly; the molecular logic applies to any genome.

**Lou DI, Hussmann JA, McBee RM, et al. (2013).** *High-throughput DNA sequencing errors are
reduced by orders of magnitude using circle sequencing.* PNAS 110:19872–19877.
[doi:10.1073/pnas.1319590110](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1319590110)

> Rolling-circle consensus. Look at the error rate before and after, and at which errors
> consensus cannot remove.

## Reference material to keep open

- Your polymerase's datasheet: error rate, proofreading, and uracil tolerance
- [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts) for
  strand-displacing and uracil-tolerant polymerases
- [NGS 101](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/): the protocol collection this course
  draws its examples from
